description:
Paradigm Shifters is on a mission to break conventional limits and build solutions that actually matter. We are Electronics and Communication Engineering builders driven by hardware design, micro-controllers, and turning raw code into real-world tech. We aren't just here to pitch an entry; we’re building a scalable, high-impact approach to tackling complex cosmic and terrestrial problems.

Why team up with us? You’ll get to work in a fast-moving, execution-first environment where creative prototyping meets solid engineering, and every member’s ideas directly shape the final build.
summary:
The SPHEREx Sky Viewer is a web-based educational platform that lets university students explore real
infrared sky imagery from NASA's SPHEREx mission. Users select targets from a built-in catalog of
famous objects (Barnard's Star, Proxima Centauri, Andromeda, Orion Nebula, the Pleiades, Crab Nebula,
and more) or enter custom coordinates (Right Ascension, Declination, Field of View). The platform
emphasizes time-based comparison and discovery: a Play/Blink control flashes between the first and last
frames, a "Subtract First & Last" tool highlights moving objects, and an AI Analyze Image feature uses
Google Gemini to detect objects and draw bounding boxes. An Aladin sky map overlay with Gaia and
WISE catalog layers enables cross-verification. With Google sign-in and a Community Findings section,
the site makes infrared astronomy approachable for students, amateurs, and researchers to find
high-proper-motion stars, brown dwarfs, and variable objects — and share discoveries.
details:
The SPHEREx Sky Viewer is a web-based "International Discovery Platform" for exploring infrared sky

images from NASA's SPHEREx mission and spotting objects that move or change over time. It lets you

pick a target from a built-in catalog of famous objects (fast-moving stars and brown dwarfs like Barnard's

Star and WISE 0855, variable stars like RW Aurigae and R Draconis, and showpieces like M31

Andromeda, the Orion Nebula, the Pleiades, Sirius, Proxima Centauri, the Crab Nebula and the Sombrero

Galaxy), or enter custom coordinates (Right Ascension, Declination and Field of View in degrees). You can

then fetch observation frames, optionally filtered by date (such as 2026W20) or detector band (such as 2A

or 4D3), with 2–10 frames per page.

Its core ideas are time-based comparison and discovery: a Play/Blink control flashes between the first and

last images with adjustable speed (FPS), "Subtract First & Last" computes the difference between two

frames so moving objects stand out, an "AI Analyze Image" feature uses Google's Gemini to detect objects

and draw bounding boxes, and an Aladin overlay opens a professional sky map centered on your

coordinates, with Gaia and WISE catalog layers for cross-checking. A Google sign-in and a "Community

Findings" section let users post and browse discoveries (it currently shows none). Overall, the site aims to

make infrared astronomy data approachable, so that students, amateurs and researchers can find

high-proper-motion stars, brown dwarfs and variable objects and share what they find.
